item.title: Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities
item.description:
Two frameworks advance zero-shot robot navigation capabilities

Recent research introduces two distinct frameworks addressing key challenges in zero-shot robot navigation: RPSI-Nav for recursive policy self-improvement in multi-object search, and ROMUX for navigation using uncalibrated exocentric cameras.

🧩 How RPSI-Nav Works

RPSI-Nav forms a recursive loop where the system revises both its navigation program and the revision mechanism itself:

  • Diagnoses search behavior and requests diagnostic views when observations cannot distinguish competing causes
  • Generates targeted navigation revisions based on diagnosis
  • Links feedback from subsequent goal searches to the rules that produced revisions
  • Updates the improver (diagnosis, observation acquisition, revision planning) to govern future improvements
  • Conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals

🧩 How ROMUX Works

ROMUX predicts metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images without camera calibration:

  • Trains a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict obstacle maps from exocentric images
  • Does not condition image tokens on camera information (pose or intrinsics)
  • Uses a small PPO-trained policy to navigate on predicted maps toward goal coordinates relative to the robot
  • Works with single or multiple cameras with partial views
  • Transfers zero-shot to real robots with cameras at varying positions and orientations across room layouts

⚙️ Key Details

Framework Task Key Innovation
RPSI-Nav Zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation Recursive self-improvement of both policy and improvement mechanism
ROMUX Point-goal navigation with obstacle avoidance Cross-view transformer predicting metric maps from uncalibrated, unknown exocentric cameras

💡 Why It Matters

  • RPSI-Nav addresses the constraint where fixed human-designed revision mechanisms limit continued self-improvement in navigation policies
  • ROMUX eliminates time-consuming calibration requiring specialized personnel, which must be repeated when cameras move or new rooms are navigated
  • Both systems operate zero-shot in unseen environments without training or fine-tuning
  • Benchmark experiments and real-robot evaluations validate both approaches
  • ROMUX matches success rates of policies using robot-mounted cameras in simulation with randomized cameras per episode

🚀 Availability

  • RPSI-Nav: Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations completed
  • ROMUX: Benchmarked in simulation with per-episode camera randomization; transferred zero-shot to real robot across various room layouts and camera positions/orientations

#robotics #navigation #zero-shot #embodied-ai #computer-vision #self-improvement

Source: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation Source: Navigating Robots from Unknown and Uncalibrated Exocentric Cameras via Map Estimation

item.title: RealtimeBench and TORSI Boost Real‑Time Performance of LLM Agents
item.description:
RealtimeBench and TORSI Boost Real‑Time Performance of LLM Agents

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late.

🔍 Overview

  • The need: evaluate agents while the world keeps moving, not just when it is paused.
  • Goal: enable powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

🎮 RealtimeBench

  • Introduced a benchmark called RealtimeBench.
  • Contains 180 tasks across six game types.
  • Evaluation runs while games continue during inference, reflecting real‑time constraints.

⚙️ Two‑Timescale Offline Recursive Self‑Improvement (TORSI)

  • Slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts.
  • Teacher writes reusable instructions for a fast student.
  • The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay.
  • Validation scores determine which updates are adopted.

📈 Results

  • Paired evaluations show that GPT‑6.1‑sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when games keep running.
  • Two rounds of TORSI raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0‑100 progress scale, improving all six game types.
  • The generated instructions also improve average scores for three other models without any retuning.
  • These findings illustrate a path toward real‑time intelligence for LLM agents.

💡 Why it matters

  • Real‑time constraints are common in interactive applications (games, robotics, live assistance).
  • Organizing learning across slow offline deliberation and fast online execution allows agents to act promptly while still benefiting from deeper analysis.
  • The approach demonstrates that knowledge can be distilled into reusable instructions, extending benefits to stronger models beyond the one directly trained.

#RealtimeBench #LLMAgents #SelfImprovement #AIResearch

Source: The World Won’t Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock Source: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds Source: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering Source: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills Source: Recursive Reward Improvement via Adversarial Meta-Prompt Evolution

item.title: Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search for Coding Agents
item.description:
Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search for Coding Agents

Researchers have introduced Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), a framework designed to enhance coding performance by allowing agents to recursively modify their own implementations under strict budget constraints.

🧩 How it works

SIFT optimizes the self-improvement process by addressing the runtime bottleneck caused by evaluating candidate modifications. Instead of relying solely on time-consuming downstream benchmark task evaluations, the framework employs an LLM-as-a-judge signal. The process includes:

  • Pairwise Comparisons: An LLM judge evaluates candidate patches through pairwise comparisons.
  • Strength Modeling: Win-loss records are aggregated using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to generate strength scores.
  • Guided Exploration: Strength scores drive rank-based parent sampling within a disaggregated tree search.
  • Resource Allocation: Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved specifically for the most promising candidate nodes.

💡 Why it matters

By using judge scores to guide exploration, SIFT allows agents to improve without being bottlenecked by slow, repetitive evaluation runs. This approach results in significant performance gains on the Polyglot benchmark while reducing resource requirements, specifically regarding:

Efficiency Metric Impact of SIFT
CPU Hours Significantly lower
Wall Clock Time Significantly lower
API Cost Significantly lower

#AI #CodingAgents #MachineLearning #SelfImprovement

Source: Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search
